title: Commercial Cleaning Cost in Newcastle: What Should You Actually Be Paying?
excerpt: Most Newcastle businesses are either overpaying for cleaning they don't need, or underpaying and getting the service that reflects it. Here's what commercial cleaning actually costs in the Hunter in 2026 — and how to make sure you're not one of them.
content:
## The number everyone wants, and why it's hard to give

Google any variation of "commercial cleaning cost Newcastle" and you'll find forum threads full of contradictory answers. Some people are paying $30 an hour. Some are paying $70. Most don't really know what they should be paying — they've just agreed to whatever the cleaner quoted and hoped for the best.

This article is an attempt to fix that.

The honest answer is that commercial cleaning costs in Newcastle depend on four things: what you're cleaning, how often, who by, and what the space is like. Strip any one of those out of the equation and the number is meaningless.

Here's how to work out whether you're on the right side of the deal.

## What drives the price

**Frequency is the biggest variable.** A five-day-a-week clean on a 200m² office will cost roughly three to four times what a twice-weekly clean costs. This isn't because the cleaner is charging more per hour — it's because there are fixed setup costs (site induction, key collection, scope documentation) that get amortised across the contract. Once those are absorbed, more visits means more hours at roughly the same per-hour rate.

**The type of facility matters a lot.** A standard professional office in Charlestown or Hamilton is the baseline. Add in clinical infection control requirements (medical and allied health), food handling areas (hospitality and restaurants), or specialist equipment, and the price moves up accordingly. Childcare cleaning sits in the middle — strict product requirements and additional safety protocols push the price above standard office but below clinical.

**Who's doing it matters as much as what.** This is the part most business owners skip. A quote from an operator who employs their cleaners directly and supervises them properly will usually be higher than a quote from someone running a casualised workforce with minimal oversight. The difference isn't a mark-up — it's what you're actually paying for: reliability, consistency, and someone who shows up.

**Your access situation affects the price too.** If cleaners can access the space after hours independently, it's simpler and cheaper than a daytime-only clean that requires coordination with your team.

## 2026 Newcastle and Hunter Valley benchmarks

These are ranges based on what we're seeing in the market — not guarantees, but a useful reference point to check your own quotes against.

**Offices, professional services (law firms, accountants, agencies):**

- 200m², three days a week: $900–$1,400/month
- 200m², five days a week: $1,400–$2,100/month
- 400m², three days a week: $1,600–$2,400/month

**Medical and allied health:**

- Clinical-grade disinfection protocols add roughly 20–30% to comparable office pricing
- 150m², five days a week: $1,800–$2,600/month

**Childcare centres:**

- Toy sanitising, cot care, non-toxic product requirements push prices to a comparable range
- 200m², five days a week: $1,500–$2,200/month

**Post-construction:**

- One-off deep cleans, typically quoted as a project price
- 300m² new fitout: $1,800–$3,500 depending on construction debris levels

These are broad ranges. Your space will be different. Get a site-specific quote.

## The per-square-metre trap

Some cleaners quote by the square metre. It sounds clean and simple, but it's usually not the right way to price a commercial clean. A 200m² office with ten bathrooms, a full kitchen, and a reception area is not the same job as a 200m² open-plan space with two bathrooms and a kitchenette. The first one takes significantly longer.

Ask your cleaner to walk the space and quote based on their assessment of actual time, not a formula applied from the car park.

If they won't visit your site before quoting, that's worth knowing about them.

## What you're actually buying when you pay for cleaning

The price you pay covers three things:

**The cleaner's time.** The visible part.

**Management and quality control.** Site audits, supervisor reviews, account management. A company that charges significantly below market rate is either operating on very thin margins (risk of them going under mid-contract) or cutting corners on management. Neither is good for you.

**Insurance and compliance.** Proper public liability and workers compensation are non-negotiable. A cleaner who is underinsured or uninsured is a liability that sits with you if something goes wrong on your premises.

## Questions to ask any cleaner before you agree to a price

- Have you visited the site, or are you quoting from a floor plan?
- Who will actually be cleaning our space, and how long have they been with your company?
- Do you conduct regular quality audits, or only respond to complaints?
- What exactly is included at our agreed frequency — and what's excluded?
- Can the scope be adjusted as our needs change?

A cleaner who answers these questions confidently is worth talking to. One who deflects or gives vague answers is telling you something.

## If you're currently paying above these ranges

You might be getting good value — or you might be paying for a service you don't need. The only way to know is to get a second quote and compare the scopes, not just the prices. A cleaner who charges more and actually shows up, trains their staff, and fixes problems quickly is cheaper in the long run than a cheaper one who doesn't.
